The lecture makes five moves. The framing comes first. The spine comes second and gets the most time, because the spine is the build. Two teardowns follow, done live against the nine components. The lesson comes before the history. A loop with no stop condition keeps calling the model provider until a human intervenes, so the provider keeps billing, and nobody has settled who is responsible for what the loop did in the meantime. Evolution 0 established that the model has no state, no ground truth, and no accountability. The loop is the first structure the builder puts around the model, and the loop inherits those gaps unless the builder designs against them. A budget is the first piece of state, an observation is the first piece of ground truth, and a ledger is the first piece of accountability. Then read the design claim for this Evolution aloud, because every design claim in the course takes its shape: one sentence, and beside it the falsifiers that would disprove it (three, on this card). The prompt became a control structure in four steps over two years. With few-shot prompting, the examples in the prompt steer the completion, so the prompt works as data. With chain-of-thought, the model emits its reasoning as text, so you can read it, and latent planning appears in that text. With self-consistency, the builder samples several chains and takes a vote, which is the first evaluator and also the first time cost multiplies, by the sample count. With ReAct, the prompt interleaves reasoning with actions and observations, so the prompt is now a loop body. Chain-of-thought plans without commitment, because no step checks the reasoning against the world. ReAct adds the observation, so each reasoning step carries a piece of ground truth, and that one addition turns a generative system into an agent. [~5 min]

Read the ReAct paper as a design document. The slide shows a trace in the paper's format: thought, action, observation, thought, action, finish. Work through the nine components with the room. The build fits in a dozen lines, and the slide reads top to bottom. The loop starts with a message list. A bounded for-loop supplies the first halt. A model call returns a structured Step, so the decision is typed, and the parser rejects a malformed decision instead of the loop executing it. The loop appends every turn to the ledger before it does anything else with the turn. If the step is an answer, the loop halts. If the step is a tool, the loop calls the tool and puts the observation back into the messages. The loop then checks the cost budget. If the turns run out, the loop raises, and it never returns silently. That gives four halts, and the ledger records each one with a reason. You will run this loop twice, once against your hosted route and once against Ollama, and measure the difference. Some small models cannot produce the schema at all. That result is a finding about the model, so record it in the flight log rather than treating it as a bug in your loop. [~5 min]

Cut from slide 6 (full wording):
- Step is a Pydantic model: kind ∈ {answer, tool}, name, args, text. The model cannot emit a malformed decision; the parser rejects it and that is an observation too.
- Final answer · turn budget · cost budget · error. Each one lands in the ledger with a reason. A halt is not a failure; a silent exit is.
- Same loop against a hosted API and against Ollama's endpoint. Measure both: latency, cost, and whether the small model can produce the schema at all.

Five failures appear on day one, and each one maps to a falsifier or an abort on your card. When the loop never halts because the model never emits an answer, the turn budget stops it, and a check for repeated identical actions stops it sooner. When a tool raises and the loop swallows the exception, treat the error as an observation and halt once the error count passes a limit. When a small model cannot produce the schema, retry within a retry budget, then halt with the reason format, and log the case as a squawk rather than as a failure of the design. When the model answers with no reasoning turn before it, that run trips a falsifier on the card. When an adversarial input asks the loop to ignore its budget, the loop halts anyway, because the budget lives in code and the prompt cannot reach it. The rule for the semester follows from the last case: a budget that lives only in the prompt is a budget the model can argue away, so halts live in code and in the ledger. [~5 min]

The second teardown is AutoGPT, and this one goes on the board with the room. AutoGPT's loop takes a goal in one sentence. The model writes a task list, executes one task with search or files or code, rewrites the list from its own summary of what it did, and goes around again. The only halt was a human closing the terminal or the API key running dry. Ask the room which component was absent. Evaluation was absent, because no step checked a result before that result fed the next plan, and the model graded itself from its own summary (summary laundering, in an early form). Governance was absent, because the goal had no performance measure, no halt, and no attestation. Memory was a vector store of the model's own outputs, so a hallucinated fact came back later as retrieved truth. Planning was present and fluent, and the fluency is the uncomfortable part, because a model that writes fluent plans with no grounding produces a spiral that reads as progress from inside. AutoGPT mattered for two reasons. It stated the ambition (give a model a goal and let it run), and it gave the field its first shared record of failure. The evaluators, budgets, and human-in-the-loop designs of 2024 and 2025 reply to that spring. [~8 min]

The table puts the two side by side. In one year the loop gained an explicit plan, an open tool set, a vector memory, spawned subagents, and a daemon runtime, and it gained nothing in evaluation or governance. The reason sits in what the authors of each system built it to show. ReAct's authors built it to show that reasoning and acting improve each other, so it optimized for a benchmark and left everything else out. AutoGPT's authors built it to show that a goal is enough, so it optimized for ambition and left grounding out. Both lacked a budget, an evaluator, and a record. The operator started the reference design in January 2026 to fill that gap, two more years after the 2023 spring, and the delay shows how long the field took to act on the lesson. Your Design Analysis for this Evolution is one of these two systems. Write the one I did not do on the board. [~7 min]

The reference design began as the loop plus the thing the loop lacked, a record of intent that survives the session. On January 12th, eleven days before the operator would show the system to students, the model said that only specification matters. The operator refused: specification, methodology, and governance, all three, or the loop drifts. [Verify the quote against genesis.md.] The additions to the loop were a PRD that says what before how, an ADR that records the decision with its alternatives, a brief with allowed paths, and an append-only ledger in which every turn, gate, and attestation is an event. None of them changed the model call. Governance arrived as the missing component. The governed path you fly this Evolution is the same one: init, the PRD interview, the first ledger event, and an attestation after you have looked at the artifacts. Read gzkit's own PRD as the worked example. It is short, and it never says how. [~7 min]

The PRD gets two minutes of its own, because the line between what and how decides whether ADR-1 will record real alternatives. The PRD states what: who uses the system, which question class it answers and which it refuses, what halting correctly means for each class, what budgets apply, what the ledger must hold, and what the human attests and when. The PRD does not state how: no model, no SDK, no framework, no schema field names, no code. If your PRD specifies a framework, you have pre-decided ADR-1 without recording alternatives, which is the post-hoc rationalization ADRs exist to prevent. [~2 min]

- • Which model, which SDK, which framework (that is ADR-1, next week) / • The Step schema's field names / • Whether the loop is a for-loop or a state graph / • Any code /  / A PRD that names a framework has pre-decided the ADR without recording alternatives — post-hoc rationalization, the thing ADRs exist to prevent.

The evaluation lens has three columns. A weak Sortie 1 shows a screenshot of one happy-path run, keeps the budget in the system prompt, and writes the falsifiers after the run. A sound Sortie 1 does what the card asks: it flies three input classes, enforces budgets in code with a reason on every halt, keeps a ledger the Chase can replay, measures both routes, and freezes the card at Go. An exceptional Sortie 1 adds a run designed to fail that did fail, in the ledger, a local-model squawk logged as a squawk, the answer-without-reasoning falsifier tested with a prompt that tempts it, and a flight-log paragraph on what the SDK hid, which is the exercise from chapter ten. [~3 min]

Two lines close the lecture. Observations are perception, which means everything the loop reads back from the world is untrusted input, and that rule becomes the injection test point in a later Evolution. The framing line stands: a loop without a halt is a bill. Build one that stops, and can say why.
